open_obligations: Note that the quote tool lets debaters verify claims, which may be what makes lying hard.
Check Kenton et al.'s contrary finding that the advantage does not grow with Elo.
Do not extend the support beyond QuALITY-style evidence-grounded debates.
in.other_title: Arguing the correct answer is easier, and the advantage grows with debater persuasiveness
in.rationale: Irving et al. state debate rests on the empirical claim that lying is harder than refuting a lie. Khan et al. report debaters earn higher Elo when assigned the correct answer and that the advantage grows with aggregate Elo, which they read as truth-telling being easier than lying in QuALITY debates; the evidence is specific to a quote-verified reading comprehension setting.
in.scope: proposed SUPPORTS: whether it is harder to lie than to refute a lie, in QuALITY debates with LLM debaters and judges and a quote verification tool

open_obligations: Check whether the claim holds beyond the single illustrative SciQ debate.
Note that no judge decides the debate; the weak model learns from transcripts.
Check whether the weak model benefits when the incorrect debater wins the exchange.
in.other_title: Reliance on 'harder to lie than to refute a lie' (Irving et al. 2018) in debate
in.rationale: Irving et al. state debate's usefulness rests on the empirical claim that it is harder to lie than to refute a lie. Lang, Huang and Li state that in their illustrative SciQ debate the incorrect debater's misleading arguments are convincingly refuted, that this conforms to Irving et al.'s claim, and that debate arguments can therefore inform weak models; the evidence offered is one example debate.
in.scope: proposed DEPENDS_ON: using debate transcripts to inform weak models, relying on lies being easier to refute than to make

open_obligations: Check that the correct-vs-incorrect Elo gap in Figure 3 is significant across judges (the authors say it holds in Figure 5)
Note the authors' own limitation that RLHF-tuned debaters may have an honesty propensity, which could inflate the correct-side advantage
Check that the quote verification tool is not the main driver of the advantage, since Irving et al.'s assumption is about argument in general
in.other_title: Khan et al.'s correct-side Elo advantage in QuALITY debates supports Irving et al.'s harder-to-lie assumption
in.rationale: The authors explicitly connect their correct-assignment Elo advantage to Irving et al.'s central assumption, which is empirical support scoped to QuALITY with RLHF-trained LLM debaters and quote verification.
in.scope: proposed SUPPORTS: Whether arguing for the truth is easier than arguing for a falsehood in debate; holds for reading-comprehension debates with a verified-quote tool

open_obligations: Check the underlying evidence in Section 4.3 and Appendix G (double consultancy 75% vs debate 77%; one-turn vs two-turn accuracy)
Note that Irving et al.'s claim concerns optimal play, while these debaters are 8B models after two DPO iterations
Check whether the LLM judge's insensitivity to refutation would also hold for human judges
in.other_title: Arnesen et al. find little evidence that refutation, Irving et al.'s key mechanism, sways judges
in.rationale: Irving et al. propose refutation as the core reason debate should work (lies are easier to refute than to defend). The authors' evidence points the other way in their setting: double consultancy nearly matches debate, and one-turn debates are judged as accurately as two-turn ones. This challenges the mechanism, not debate's usefulness, and the authors hedge it ('does not yet seem', 'in our setting').
in.scope: proposed CHALLENGES: Whether explicit refutation drives judge accuracy in debate; holds for an LLM judge in information-asymmetric reading comprehension with short debates

open_obligations: Read the Figure 1 transcript to judge whether Debater A's turn-3 reply actually refutes Debater B's claims
Check whether any quantitative result in the paper (e.g. debate vs consultancy ablation) bears on the claim beyond this example
in.other_title: Lang et al. say their example debate conforms to Irving et al.'s 'harder to lie than to refute a lie'
in.rationale: The authors explicitly say their observation agrees with Irving et al.'s central claim, which is SUPPORTS. The evidence is one qualitative example, not a measured rate.
in.scope: proposed SUPPORTS: Whether honest debaters can expose false claims in LLM debate; holds only for the single illustrated transcript

text: The authors state that the usefulness of debate for alignment rests on the central claim that, in the debate game, it is harder to lie than to refute a lie, and that whether this holds in a given setting is empirical. If it holds, they hope that in all Nash equilibria both agents try to tell the truth convincingly, that approximate equilibria can be found by self-play gradient methods with stable training, and that equilibrium debaters are approximately as strong as unrestricted AI.
title: Central claim of debate: it is harder to lie than to refute a lie
